## 3. How the harness drives the system

### 3.1 report and x1: a process per stage, re-created

`--max-steps` is fixed when the interpreter starts and counts from the start
of the process, and the interpreter reports its count only when the limit
stops it. So, to give every stage and every spawned computation its own
budget of exactly 10⁶ steps (10⁸ for P12, P13, P16), the harness runs each
in its own process: for stage k of an incremental program it starts the
interpreter with `--max-steps R(k−1) + budget`, writes the instance line and
constants and `1 1`, waits for `[end]`, writes `1 2`, … and finally `1 k`.
The program receives every stage as it first arrived, one after another,
into one computation; the earlier stages are re-created, not replayed, and
the record says `posed.how = "incremental"` with nothing replayed (QUESTIONS.md
A2). **Every such attempt is marked**: its `notes` begin with a line

    recreated_for_budget: true; computation: main; prefix_messages: 2; prefix_stages: [1, 2]; prefix_steps: 103; prefix_commit_stages_carried_out_again: []

(the schema has no field for it, so it is a note in this fixed form).
`prefix_steps` is R(k−1), the steps of the re-created prefix: they are **not
charged to the stage** (`steps.stage` and the budget count from the end of
the prefix; `restart_cost` is null; `steps.restated` includes them, as
"from nothing"). A commit stage in the re-created prefix is carried out
again by the program, deterministically, and listed in
`prefix_commit_stages_carried_out_again`; its output (v included) is checked
byte-identical to the first time. This relies on the interpreter being deterministic (it has no clock and
no random numbers): the earlier stages' output in the new process must be
byte-identical to what was recorded for them, or the run has a harness fault.
Their output is not repeated in the attempt's `stdout`, and their emits are
not logged again.

**Steps** are read only through `--max-steps`, by bisection: R(k), the steps
until the program asks for input after stage k (or ends), is the least limit
at which a run of stages 1..k, its input closed after stage k's `[end]`, is
not stopped with `stopped after N steps`. Each probe is a run of the program
(their number is in the record's notes). The stage's incremental cost is
R(k) − R(k−1), its restated cost R(k).

**A reposed stage** (a reposed program; or an incremental one after budget,
error or timeout, and every safety rerun after stage 1): one new process,
all messages written at once. Its restart cost is measured as a separate run
(`restart_cost_method: "separate-run"`): the least limit at which stages
1..k−1 alone (their messages, then the input closed) are not stopped. The
budget is that plus 10⁶ (10⁸). The replay as a whole has at most the sum of
its stages' budgets (QUESTIONS.md A6).

### 3.2 x1sim: one live process

No step count, no limit. An incremental program runs in **one x1sim
process** for the whole run: the harness writes each message after the
previous `[end]`, and the computation is genuinely the same. A reposed stage
starts a new process with all its messages. x1sim writes its object file
beside the program, so it runs in a fresh temporary directory with a copy
`prog.a60`, `HOME` set there and `X1ALGOL_LIB` unset, so the library is
`/usr/local/lib/x1algol.lib`.

### 3.3 Safety limit

60 s per attempt (600 s for P12, P13, P16), as `stages.json` gives. For an
incremental attempt it runs from writing the stage's message to its `[end]`
(the re-created earlier stages are not inside it: they are guarded at 900 s
as a harness fault); for a reposed attempt it covers the whole run (Q13).
The harness stops the system with **SIGKILL to its process group**
(`how_stopped`), keeps what had been printed, and reruns once at the raised
limit (reposed; for stage 1, fresh) where the problem allows, else the stop
is final (`fixed-limit-timeout`). The interpreter flushes its output at every
read of input, at an error and at the step limit, but not when killed:
output printed but not yet flushed when the safety limit kills it is lost.

### 3.4 Modes

| mode | report, x1 | x1sim |
|---|---|---|
| behaviour | `algol60` with the budget's `--max-steps`; steps are measured only where a later budget needs them | `x1sim`, no budget |
| cost | as behaviour, plus R(k) at every stage, `steps_at` for each collected answer (the least limit at which the answer's `[/answer]` is in the output), `to_first_answer`, `between_answers`, `to_end`; repeated work from one extra run of `algol60-measure --measure` per computation | refused |
| storage | `algol60-measure --measure` for the attempt (its steps, under `--max-steps`, are the baseline's: systems file) | refused |

**Store** (storage mode): `--measure` reports at the end of the process,
after the interpreter has unwound. The totals (`frames_made`, `calls`,
`name_uses`, `name_evaluations`, `name_first_evaluations`,
`name_repeat_evaluations`) are read as the stage boundary's, since the
process ends there; the live quantities (`frames`, `slots`, `arrays`,
`array_elements`, `names`, `call_depth`) have `boundary: null`, and their
peak over the process (stages 1..k) is recorded as the stage's (`exact`)
only where it exceeds the peak at the end of stage k−1, else `null`; a
reposed stage's peak is its run's. **Repeated work** is
`name_repeat_evaluations` (with first and all evaluations) between the
boundaries, or over the whole reposed run. **P13**: `cpu_time_s` and
`max_rss_kb` are the attempt process's, from `wait4`, in behaviour and cost
mode (not storage, which is instrumented).

### 3.5 Confounds

Everything the harness does beyond passing stages in, collecting answers and
reading state (copied into every record's `run.confounds`):

1. the re-creation of the computation in report and x1 (3.1): an attempt
   in a fresh process, re-created for its budget, recorded as incremental
   and marked `recreated_for_budget: true` with its `prefix_steps`, which
   are not charged to the stage; its determinism check; a commit stage in
   the re-created prefix is carried out again by the program,
   deterministically, its output (v included) checked identical, and listed
   in the mark;
2. the bisection probes, extra runs of the program, for every step count;
3. closing the input after the stage under test, which ends the process with
   the interpreter's "input is exhausted" error after `[end]`;
4. the safety limit of an incremental attempt excludes the re-created stages;
5. output still in the interpreter's buffer at a safety-limit kill is lost;
6. store and repeated work read from the end-of-process report of the
   measurement build, with the peak attribution of 3.4;
7. the instance line and messages written on standard input, each message
   followed by its stage's constants lines with their `k:` tag removed;
8. answers, observe state, emits and stage ends read from printed tags by
   pattern matching; answers beyond the cap left uncollected;
9. spawned computations are parts of one program, run one after another;
10. x1sim: run in a temporary directory on a copy of the program, and no
    budget.

## 4. Records

`run` writes `OUTDIR/<instance>.<mode>.<UTC>.json`, then validates it with
`harnesses/validate.py`; an invalid record is kept as `….INVALID.json` and
`run` exits 3. Exit 0 whatever the outcome of the stages; 2 for a usage error
(unknown configuration, instance or mode, a mode x1sim does not have, no
posing declaration), with no record. `PROGRAM` and `OUTDIR` are relative to
the repository root. `system_build.commit` is read from `/opt/src/COMMITS`;
the image digest from `HARNESS_IMAGE` if the launcher passes it, else null.
`HARNESS_PURPOSE` sets `run.purpose` (`primary` by default); `HARNESS_STAGES`
another stages file (only the qualification uses it).

## 5. check

`harnesses/algol-60/check CONFIGURATION PROGRAM`:

| configuration | what it runs |
|---|---|
| report | `algol60 --check PROGRAM`: parses and compiles, reports errors and warnings, runs nothing |
| x1 | `algol60 --x1 --check PROGRAM`, the same in the X1 dialect |
| x1sim | `x1algc prog.a60 /usr/local/lib/x1algol.lib` on a copy, in a temporary directory: the X1 compiler alone; the object code is discarded and the simulator is never started. On failure the compiler's report (which it writes on standard output) is printed |

It also reports whether the posing declaration is present and whether a
constants file is beside the program. Messages are printed verbatim; exit 0
if none is an error, 1 otherwise. It poses no stage and prints nothing the
program would compute. The X1 compiler finds fewer errors than `algol60
--check` (it accepted `k := 1 +;`, which then stopped at run time); an x1sim
author may also check the program in x1. The qualification (E1–E2) shows a
program whose only effect is to print a marker leaves no marker and no file
when checked, in all three configurations.

## 6. Qualification

`qualification/qualify.py`, run in the image from the repository root,
reruns all of it on made-up programs and problems (X01–X09,
`qualification/stages-made-up.json`) and writes its records to
`qualification/records/<UTC>/`. Its output is `qualification/output.txt`.
It shows: (A) the system run directly and the harness agree on each stage's
output and answers, the harness's step counts agree with `--max-steps`
itself (R passes, R−1 stops), the systems file's step examples (3, 3, 5, 1)
are reproduced as stage-step differences, and the storage figures equal
`--measure` run directly; (B) incremental and reposed programs give the same
answers in all three configurations, a commitment is replayed verbatim, the
modes agree, spawn follows the instance's order; (C) budget, error, safety
rerun, final and fixed-limit timeouts and usage errors; (D) every record

# Protocol
*Draft 0.7.*
## Phases
1. **Draft.** `SPECIFICATION.md`, `METRICS.md`, this file and `problems/`
   are written. No program for the study is written, apart from the
   calibration programs (`METRICS.md`, Calibration), which are development
   examples and never results.
   Measurement may be qualified at this phase: establishing what each
   system can report, and adding instrumentation that changes no result,
   under the conditions in "Instrumentation" below.
2. **Independent review.** A reviewer who has not written the draft reads
   it for ambiguity, for errors in the valid outcomes, for language bias,
   and for problems missing from the suite. Findings and responses are kept
   in `reviews/`. *(Draft 0.1 had one review, answered in draft 0.2. Draft
   0.3 had a second, by a fresh reviewer, answered in draft 0.4. Draft 0.5
   had a third, answered in draft 0.6. Draft 0.7 is the freeze candidate.)*
3. **Freeze.** The specification is tagged `spec-1.0`, together with:
   - the pinned version or commit of every system in the first comparison;
   - each systems file's cores, flags and units;
   - the generic harness interface below.
   From then on, these change only by amendment.
4. **Harnesses.** One harness per system implements the interface, and is
   published before any program is run.
5. **Implementation.** Programs are written for each configuration from the
   problem files, one per configuration and problem, fixed before any of
   them is run.
6. **Results.** Each program is run and classified, and the results are
   recorded in `results/`.
7. **Comparison.** Only after results exist for at least two systems on
   every problem.
No system is implemented before the freeze. The benchmark is not changed
afterwards to suit any system, including PLANNER and the systems after it.
## Amendments
An amendment is a numbered, dated change to a frozen file, with its reason.
It applies to every system. Results obtained before it are kept, marked
with the specification version they were obtained under, and rerun under
the new version.
A problem proposed after the freeze does not join the frozen suite. It goes
into a separate, dated supplementary suite, reported apart from the frozen
one, with the date it was proposed and the results that existed then.
## Roles
| role | does | has access to |
|---|---|---|
| **specification author** | writes the problems and the protocol | the public repository |
| **variant custodian** | writes the hidden variants and their valid outcomes | the specification, and the private variants |
| **implementation author** | writes the programs | the public repository only |
| **harness author** | writes each system's harness (phase 4) | the public repository |
| **classifier A** | classes the programs' constructs, and the outcomes of every run on all axes, checking residual equivalence | the specification, the metrics, the programs, their outputs and the valid outcomes |
| **classifier B** | does both independently | the same, without A's classes |
| **verifier** | runs the programs on the hidden variants | the programs, the variants and their outcomes |
Each role is a separate agent or person, with its own context, and its
provenance is recorded. The two classifiers are of different origin (for
instance Claude and Codex), and neither wrote the program it classes.
Their disagreements, on tokens and on outcomes, are recorded, and a
disputed outcome is reported under both classes.
**Hidden variants** are made inaccessible, not merely placed where an
implementation author is told not to look. *(For wave 1, amended:
`AMENDMENTS.md`, 1.)* The custodian writes them
before the freeze and encrypts them with a key the project's owner holds
but does not use. The plaintext begins with a random nonce of at least 128
bits, so that a small space of constants cannot be recovered from its
hash. Only the ciphertext and the SHA-256 hash of the plaintext are
committed. The key is given to the verifier only after every primary
program and its results are committed. The verifier publishes the
plaintext, and anyone can check it against the hash. Each later wave of
systems (PLANNER onwards) has its own sealed set, made before that wave's
programs are written, since revealing a set publishes it.
## Evidence classification
Every implementation is given one or more of these classes:
| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| **original** | a surviving historical implementation, on the hardware or software it was written for |
| **rehosted** | a surviving historical implementation, running in a modern environment (an emulator, a port of the original source) |
| **reconstructed** | a modern implementation derived from historical documents, where no implementation survives |
| **modern** | a contemporary implementation of the language |
| **extended** | mechanisms supplied for the experiment, beyond the implementation's own |
Two qualifiers may be attached to a class:
- *with external mechanisms*: libraries or run-time features outside the
  configuration's core are used (`METRICS.md`);
- *alternative reading*: a reconstruction run with a decision taken the
  other way, where its sources conflict.
Results are always reported with the class. No result from a modern or
extended configuration is attributed to the historical language. Where a
language was described more fully than it was implemented (PLANNER and
Micro-Planner, for instance), the described language and the implemented
subset are separate systems.
## Configurations
A configuration is one system with a stated set of mechanisms. Results are
kept separate per configuration, so that a capability introduced later is
not attributed to the earlier model. Each systems file lists, per
configuration:
- its core, built-in by built-in;
- its flags;
- the unit of steps, of an alternative and of store, and how each is
  measured;
- what "the same computation" means. That is, whether a stage can be
  received into a computation already running, and how.
A reconstruction is pinned at a commit when the specification is frozen.
Any later change to it, for whatever reason, makes a new configuration,
reported separately, and never replaces the pinned one.
## Instrumentation
A measurement added to a system must not change what it computes. For a
reconstruction:
- the unmodified commit is kept as the baseline;
- instrumentation is made on a separate branch, and recorded as its own
  commit;
- it may not change scheduling, search, equality, suspension or any other
  rule of the machine;
- the instrumented build, with measurement on and off, must give output
  identical to the baseline's, byte for byte, on every example and in every
  output mode, including full traces. The check and its result are
  recorded.
## The harness interface
Every harness provides exactly these operations, and nothing that orders,
chooses or re-poses goals on its own:
- **pose(stage)**: give the system the information of one stage, into the
  same computation if the configuration allows it, or else by reposing.
  A reposed run replays **every** stage 1 to k in order, replacements and
  withdrawals included, and the program must carry them out. The harness
  never works out the net information itself;
- **spawn(computation)**: start a separate computation in the same
  instance (P09), returning at once where the configuration can run
  computations side by side. In a configuration that cannot, the first
  runs to its end or its budget, and then the next;
- **answers(cap)**: collect the answers the system reports, through its
  standard mechanism for enumerating them, until it is exhausted, the
  budget runs out, or `cap` answers have been collected. `cap` is 1 for an
  *any one* query and 20 otherwise, as each problem states. The execution
  state is classified after the call;
- **observe()**: record the state the common observations need, including
  bindings the system holds (`SPECIFICATION.md`, "reported");
- **print()**.
Each system's systems file says what its standard mechanism for answers
is. For Python and ALGOL 60, it is the values the program prints.
**Observing must not consume the computation.** In a system where
collecting answers would end or alter the computation that the next stage
extends (exhausting a backtracking search, for instance), the observation
of stage k is taken on a separate run of stages 1 to k. The incremental
run is left as it was.
**Commitments are preserved when a run is reposed.** When a commit stage
has selected an outcome v (P11), a reposed run replays it as the
information x = v. It does not ask the system to select again, which could
commit to a different outcome.
**External effects** (P11) are written to one log per problem, never reset,
across every run the harness makes for classification, reposed runs
included. Separate observation runs write to a separate log, which is not
judged. Entries that are duplicated only because a run was reposed are
counted separately, as the cost of reposing an irreversible effect.
Concurrency used to run computations (threads, processes) is a mechanism of
the configuration, listed in its systems file. A harness may not run
computations concurrently itself. In P09, all computations run in one
instance of the system, sharing one database, never in separate operating
system processes.
## Writing a program
1. Write it from the problem file. Programs written for this study's
   precursors (the absys experiments E01–E09) exist, and their author may
   have seen them; each program says whether its author had.
2. Use the idioms of the system's period where they are known. Cite the
   source of each idiom: a manual, a paper or a published program.
3. Transcribe the definitions given. Anything else is reformulation, and
   counts as R.
4. Where several idiomatic programs are possible, choose one per
   configuration and problem before any is run, or run and report every
   variant. In either case, one is designated the **primary** variant
   before any is run, and stands for the configuration.
5. **No anticipation.** The code that handles stage k may not depend on the
   content of any later stage.
6. **Genericity.** A program must stay correct when the constants in a
   problem's stages are changed. It keeps them in one marked place, or reads
   them as input, so that the verifier can substitute them. Each problem
   has hidden variants with other constants, held by someone who does not
   write programs. Every program is run on them after its results are
   recorded. The custodian works out each variant's valid outcomes
   independently, stage by stage, as the problem files give them for the
   original constants. A variant's outcomes need not have the same classes
   as the original's: other constants can make a finite outcome infinite,
   or a consistent stage inconsistent. A program's run on a variant is
   classified against **that variant's** valid outcomes, on the semantic and
   effects axes, exactly as a primary run is. A program **fails** a variant
   where that classification differs from its classification on the
   original constants, each against its own valid outcomes: a program
   complete on the original and unsound on the variant fails it. It is
   recorded as such, since it encodes a conclusion rather than computing
   it. The custodian records, for each variant, which of the original's
   outcome classes it was built to keep, if any.
7. A program may not be revised after its results are seen, except to fix a
   transcription error: a place where the program departs from the text of
   the problem file. Each fix is recorded as a diff, with the reason. A
   program changed for any other reason is a separate, named variant, and
   is reported as such.
8. Record the author of each program, human or agent.
## Running
- Pin the version of every system, and record its source and commit.
- **Budget.** 10⁶ steps in the system's own unit, per stage and per
  computation. In P09, each separate computation has its own budget and its
  own classification. A reposed run of stages 1 to k has a budget of its
  measured restart cost plus 10⁶.
- **The budget is relative to each system.** 10⁶ Absys steps, SWI-Prolog
  inferences and Python instructions are different amounts of work. So
  *budget* is a classification within a system, and is not compared
  across systems. Each system records, as a calibration figure, its steps
  for P13b at n = 10³, or, where P13b is not expressible, for P03e.
- **After budget.** If stage k ends in *budget* and the configuration can
  keep its computation and continue it, stage k+1 is posed into that same
  computation, with a new budget. Whether it can is recorded, since
  continuing past an exhausted budget is itself a capability. Stages 1 to
  k+1 are reposed only when the configuration cannot continue, and the
  reposing counts under restart cost.
- **After error.** Stage k+1 is posed by reposing stages 1 to k+1, counted
  under restart cost.
- **Safety limit.** A limit of 60 seconds per stage protects the harness.
  It is not a measurement. A stage it stops is rerun once, with the limit
  raised tenfold. If the rerun also stops, *timeout* is final for that
  stage. Both runs are recorded. Answers reported before the limit stopped
  the run are kept and classified on the semantic axis; only the execution
  state is *timeout*.
## Modes of running
Each program is run in up to three modes:
| mode | what it establishes | instrumentation |
|---|---|---|
| **behaviour** | the outcomes, the three axes and effects | none beyond the harness |
| **cost** | steps, answer latency, problem-defined operation counts | step counting only |
| **storage** | store, retained alternatives, suspended state | the systems file's storage measurement |
- The semantic result and execution state are taken from the behaviour run.
- Where two modes can be compared, their semantic results must agree, and
  any disagreement is reported as a fault of the instrumentation.
- A sampled measurement is never taken from the run that gives the step
  count or the classification, because sampling adds steps of its own.
- A run that hits the safety limit only because it is instrumented (in
  cost or storage mode, when the behaviour run finished) is not evidence
  that the model cannot complete the problem. It is recorded as a limit of
  the measurement.
- Run in CI where the system allows it, and compare with recorded output.
## Recording a result
Each result is a file `results/<system>/<configuration>/<problem>.md` that
gives:
- the specification version, the system version or commit, the
  configuration and the evidence class;
- the program, or a link to it at a commit, and whether its author had seen
  a precursor;
- for each stage, the common observations of `SPECIFICATION.md` and the
  problem's own;
- the token counts by class, per classifier, with the disputed tokens;
- the configuration's expressibility for the problem;
- the supporting code (S) used, by mechanism. An *extended* result is named
  by its mechanism. Every configuration's S mechanisms are listed, with
  their size, at phase 4, before any program is run;
- whether the program passed its hidden variants.
## Guarding against bias
- The reasons for choosing a problem, and the history of each system's
  implementation, are disclosed.
- Every review is asked for problems that favour designs other than those
  the suite came from.
- Results are reported for every system on every problem, including
  "not expressible".
- Both classifiers' token classes are kept and reported for every result,
  throughout the study, never only an adjudicated set. A comparative
  conclusion that would change if one classifier's classes were used in
  place of the other's is reported as **classification-sensitive**, with
  both figures.
- No ranking is computed. A summary may say where a system needed control,
  supporting code or intervention that another did not, and what it held in
  store to avoid them.
- Interpretation, including any connection to later work, is kept out of
  `results/` and in a separate document written after the comparison.

"""Segment a token file into atoms (small constructs) for classing.

An atom is a run of tokens forming one construct at the finest grain used:
a simple statement, a conditional's header (if ... then), an else, a for
header (for ... do), a begin, an end (with its end-comment), a procedure
heading with its value and specification parts, a declaration item.
A separator ';' starts the atom after it (METRICS.md rule 20).
"""
import csv, sys

TYPEKW = {"integer", "Boolean", "boolean", "real"}


def load(path):
    toks = []
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        r = csv.reader(f, delimiter="\t", quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE)
        next(r)
        for row in r:
            toks.append((int(row[0]), int(row[1]), row[2]))
    for i, t in enumerate(toks):
        assert t[0] == i
    return toks


def atoms(toks):
    """Return list of (start, end) inclusive index ranges."""
    out = []
    n = len(toks)
    i = 0
    cur = None

    def close(upto):
        nonlocal cur
        if cur is not None and cur <= upto:
            out.append((cur, upto))
        cur = None

    while i < n:
        t = toks[i][2]
        if t == ";":
            close(i - 1)
            cur = i
            i += 1
            continue
        if t == "begin":
            # a pending lone ';' joins begin
            if cur is not None and toks[cur][2] == ";" and cur == i - 1:
                out.append((cur, i)); cur = None
            else:
                close(i - 1); out.append((i, i))
            i += 1
            continue
        if t == "end":
            if cur is not None and toks[cur][2] == ";" and cur == i - 1:
                # empty statement before end: attach ';' to end
                start = cur; cur = None
            else:
                close(i - 1); start = i
            j = i + 1
            while j < n and toks[j][2] not in (";", "end", "else"):
                j += 1
            out.append((start, j - 1))
            i = j
            continue
        if t == "else":
            close(i - 1)
            if i + 1 < n and toks[i + 1][2] == "if":
                j = i + 1
                while toks[j][2] != "then":
                    j += 1
                out.append((i, j)); i = j + 1
            else:
                out.append((i, i)); i += 1
            continue
        if t == "if" and (cur is None or toks[cur][2] == ";" and cur == i - 1 or cur is not None):
            # if a statement is in progress and is an assignment with a
            # conditional expression (x := if ...), keep it in the statement
            if cur is not None and any(toks[k][2] == ":=" for k in range(cur, i)):
                i += 1
                continue
            start = cur if (cur is not None and cur == i - 1 and toks[cur][2] == ";") else None
            close(i - 1) if start is None else None
            if start is None:
                start = i
            cur = None
            j = i
            depth = 0
            while toks[j][2] != "then" or depth:
                if toks[j][2] == "if" and j != i:
                    depth += 1
                if toks[j][2] == "then" and depth:
                    depth -= 1
                j += 1
            out.append((start, j)); i = j + 1
            continue
        if t == "for":
            start = cur if (cur is not None and cur == i - 1 and toks[cur][2] == ";") else None
            if start is None:
                close(i - 1); start = i
            cur = None
            j = i
            while toks[j][2] != "do":
                j += 1
            out.append((start, j)); i = j + 1
            continue
        if t == "procedure" or (t in TYPEKW and i + 1 < n and toks[i + 1][2] == "procedure"):
            start = cur if (cur is not None and cur == i - 1 and toks[cur][2] == ";") else None
            if start is None:
                close(i - 1); start = i
            cur = None
            j = i
            while toks[j][2] != ";":
                j += 1
            # value and specification parts
            while j + 1 < n and (toks[j + 1][2] == "value" or (toks[j + 1][2] in TYPEKW and toks[j + 2][2] != "procedure" and toks[j + 2][2] != "array")):
                j += 1
                while toks[j][2] != ";":
                    j += 1
            out.append((start, j)); i = j + 1
            continue
        if cur is None:
            cur = i
        i += 1
    close(n - 1)
    # check cover
    seen = []
    for a, b in out:
        seen.extend(range(a, b + 1))
    assert seen == list(range(n)), "atoms do not cover"
    return out

    toks = load(sys.argv[1])
    for k, (a, b) in enumerate(atoms(toks)):
        print(k, toks[a][1], " ".join(t[2] for t in toks[a:b + 1]))

import sys, json, collections
sys.path.insert(0,'.')
from classify import classify, TOK, FAMILY
texts = ["report/P07a.alg","report/P07b.alg","report/P07c.alg","report/P07d.alg","report/P07f.alg","report/P07g.alg","report/P08a.alg","report/P08c.alg",

out = {}
totals = {}
for t in texts:
    f = t.split("/")[1][:4]
    toks, ats, tx, cls, info, proc = classify(TOK + t + ".tokens.tsv", FAMILY[f])
    spans = []
    cover = [0]*len(toks)
    for i,(a,b) in enumerate(ats):
        assert cls[i] in "PCRSH" and len(cls[i])==1, (t, tx[i], cls[i])

    assert all(c==1 for c in cover), t
    out[t] = spans
    c = collections.Counter()
    for s in spans: c[s["class"]] += s["to"]-s["from"]+1
    totals[t] = dict(sorted(c.items())) | {"total": len(toks)}
json.dump(out, open("tokens.json","w"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=0)
for t,v in totals.items(): print(t, v)

"""Residual equivalence checks for algol-60 P07 and P08 (classifier A).

P07: each reported residual or answer is checked against the valid
outcomes by enumerating integer assignments in a window (|v| <= 60); the
residual relations are parsed from the record's observe block.
P08: the reported bindings and held equations are closed under the held
element equations (union-find) and compared, term by term, with the
valid outcomes' solved form.
Run: python3 -I equiv.py  (prints one line per check; exit 1 on a failure)
"""
import itertools, sys

W = range(-60, 61)
ok = True


def check(name, cond):
    global ok
    print(("PASS " if cond else "FAIL ") + name)
    ok = ok and cond


# ---- P07 ----
def sols2(rel):
    return {(x, y) for x in W for y in W if rel(x, y)}


# P07b residual: x + y = 10, x - y = 4 held  vs valid x = 7, y = 3
check("P07b residual {x+y=10, x-y=4} == {(7,3)}", sols2(lambda x, y: x + y == 10 and x - y == 4) == {(7, 3)})
# P07c residual: x + y = 10 held vs valid: every pair with x + y = 10 (identical relation)
check("P07c residual {x+y=10} == valid (same relation, window)", sols2(lambda x, y: x + y == 10) == {(x, 10 - x) for x in W if 10 - x in W})
# P07f residual: x + y = 10, x + y = 11 held vs none
check("P07f residual {x+y=10, x+y=11} == {} (inconsistency undetected)", sols2(lambda x, y: x + y == 10 and x + y == 11) == set())
# P07a explicit answers, every order: x=5,y=4,z=3
check("P07a x=5,y=4,z=3 is the only solution", {(x, y, z) for x in W for y in W for z in W if x + y + z == 12 and y + z == 7 and z == 3} == {(5, 4, 3)})
# P07d explicit
check("P07d w=7 (u=2,v=14) only", {w for w in W if w * 2 == 14} == {7})
# P07e reported none
check("P07e none: no integer w with 2w = 15", {w for w in W if w * 2 == 15} == set())
# P07g both roots
check("P07g x*x=9 -> {3,-3}", {x for x in W if x * x == 9} == {3, -3})


# ---- P08 ----
class UF:
    def __init__(self):
        self.p = {}

    def f(self, a):
        self.p.setdefault(a, a)
        while self.p[a] != a:
            a = self.p[a]
        return a

    def u(self, a, b):
        self.p[self.f(a)] = self.f(b)


def close(seq, eqs):
    uf = UF()
    for a, b in eqs:
        uf.u(a, b)
    return [uf.f(e) if isinstance(e, str) else e for e in seq]


def same_up_to(rep_terms, rep_eqs, valid_terms, valid_eqs):
    """Both sides denote the same set if, under each side's equations, the
    terms coincide and each side's equations are entailed by the other's."""
    a = [close(t, rep_eqs) for t in rep_terms]
    b = [close(t, rep_eqs) for t in valid_terms]
    c = [close(t, valid_eqs) for t in rep_terms]
    d = [close(t, valid_eqs) for t in valid_terms]
    ent1 = all(close([x], valid_eqs) == close([y], valid_eqs) for x, y in rep_eqs)
    ent2 = all(close([x], rep_eqs) == close([y], rep_eqs) for x, y in valid_eqs)
    return a == b and c == d and ent1 and ent2


# stage 3 (open): reported a=(x,y,z), x = y held, rev pending; valid a=(y,y,z), x=y, rev pending
check("P08a s3 open: a=(x,y,z) & x=y  ==  a=(y,y,z) & x=y",
      same_up_to([["x", "y", "z"]], [("x", "y")], [["y", "y", "z"]], [("x", "y")]))
# stage 4: reported a=(x,y,z), b=(z,y,x), x=y held; valid x=y, a=(y,y,z), b=(z,y,y)
check("P08a s4: a=(x,y,z), b=(z,y,x), x=y  ==  a=(y,y,z), b=(z,y,y), x=y",
      same_up_to([["x", "y", "z"], ["z", "y", "x"]], [("x", "y")], [["y", "y", "z"], ["z", "y", "y"]], [("x", "y")]))
# stage 5: reported a=(x,y,z), b=(z,y,x), x=y, y=z held; valid x=y=z, a=b=(z,z,z)
check("P08a s5: a=(x,y,z), b=(z,y,x), x=y, y=z  ==  a=b=(z,z,z), x=y=z",
      same_up_to([["x", "y", "z"], ["z", "y", "x"]], [("x", "y"), ("y", "z")], [["z", "z", "z"], ["z", "z", "z"]], [("x", "y"), ("y", "z")]))
# stage 6 explicit
check("P08a s6: (42,42,42) reversed is itself, and (42) ++ c = b gives c = (42,42)",
      list(reversed([42, 42, 42])) == [42, 42, 42] and [42, 42, 42][1:] == [42, 42])
# P08c stage 4
check("P08c s4: rev((1,2)) = (2,1)", list(reversed([1, 2])) == [2, 1])

sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)

# Classifier A, algol-60, batch 1B (P07–P08): notes

Classifier A (a Claude agent). Clone at commit 3c7c778, not modified. Output
`algol-60.json` beside this file. The scripts are here too: `atoms.py` cuts each
token file into constructs, `classify.py` classes them (rules and per-program
overrides, each with its METRICS.md rule), `tokens_out.py` writes and checks the
spans, `summ.py`, `beh.py` and `modes.py` read the records, `equiv.py` checks
the residuals, `build.py` assembles the JSON, and `verify.py` checks coverage.
`show-*.txt` are the construct-by-construct listings I reviewed.

## Texts

There are 16 texts, each classed once under the first path in
`TEXTS-1B-P07-P08.tsv`. `report/P07d.alg` also stands for P07e, `report/P08a.alg`
for P08b, and each `x1/*.a60` for its identical `x1sim` file. No class differs
between configurations: S-mechanisms.md lists no S mechanism in any of them, and
the x1 and x1sim files are byte-identical. So nothing is classed a second time.
The report and x1 texts have the same structure line for line. Only the input
and output statements differ (`ininteger`/`outstring` against `read`/`PRINTTEXT`/`NLCR`).
I checked that every line's set of classes is the same in the two dialects (`cmp.py`).

## Constructs that were hard to class, and the reading I took

1. **The holding code (rule 19).** Every program holds its relations in
   problem-specific code: an `examineN` evaluator per relation, `equal`, and a
   `propagate` fixpoint loop. I classed it R. Inside the evaluators I split
   them by rule 19:
   - P: computing a place (`xv := c1 - yv - zv`, `vv ÷ uv` with its
     divisibility test, `av := cons(...)`, the decomposition of b = s ++ c),
     and the test of a fully known relation with its verdict
     (`if … ≠ c1 then inconsistent := true`).
   - R: the knownness tests (`if xk ∧ yk then`, `if ek[e] ∨ ek[f] then`),
     `xk := true`, `rN := false`/`qN := false` and `changed := true`.

   Three points are open to dispute:
   - I classed the evaluator's procedure heading and its begin/end R, as
     part of the holding code. One could argue they are P, as the relation's
     "definition".
   - I classed `propagate`, all of it including its order dispatch on `ord[j]`
     in P07a, R by rule 19. A reader could class the fixpoint loop C
     ("explicit scheduling").
   - I classed the `ord` array and its declaration R. The instance line's
     order drives the examination order. Reading it from the input is H
     (harness README 2.7.1).
2. **The unknowns' representation.** I classed the value variables (xv, av,
   ev, xs, nx and the like) P, as the unknowns. I classed the "known" flags
   (xk, ak, ek) R, as holding state. A multiple assignment mixes the two
   (`xk := yk := zk := inconsistent := false`). It is one construct, so it
   takes one class, R. Likewise `top := rev1 := rev2 := conc1 := conc2 := 0`
   mixes the cell allocator with four counters. I classed it P, because it
   initialises the encoding (rule 13: it computes something the report
   depends on, so it is not H).
3. **`inconsistent`** is P: its declaration, its initialisation, and its
   setting by a test. **`held`** and its computation are H. I read them as
   collecting, for observe, what the program already holds (rule 13). They
   are close to the line, because the observe block depends on them. The
   guard `if ¬inconsistent then` around the answer printing in the main
   program is H, because it only chooses what to print. The same test
   inside `examine6` is P: it decides whether c is given a value.
4. **P08's late definition.** The flags `defined`, `concdef`, `rev1def` and
   `rev2def`, their setting at the defining stage, and the guards on them
   are R, by rule 19. The program says it holds "the application of a
   relation not yet defined until it can be decided". Rule 11 makes a
   *declaration* that changes how an undefined relation behaves C. These
   flags are code, not a declaration, but they do choose the open reading.
   A classifier who reads rule 11 broadly would class them C. This is
   ambiguous and could matter for the C/R split of P08.
5. **P08c's status protocol.** I classed rev and conc's "found / none /
   cannot tell" results R: `conc := 1`, `st`, `t`, the `if t = 1 then`
   tests, and `st := if rev1def ∧ rev2def then 0 else 2`. They are an extra
   result, which rule 3 treats as an extra argument, and they make the
   wait verdict. The case bodies (the head tests `same(a, pv)` and
   `a ≠ 0`, and the conjunct calls) are P, by rules 2 and 3. The guard
   `if st ≠ 1 ∧ rev2def then` combines a commitment to case 1 with the
   arrival flag. It is one construct; I classed it R.
6. **P08c case 1 as data.** rev's case 1 `rev(⟨⟩, ⟨⟩)` is read at stage 3 as
   two constant sequences p and r (`3: 0 0`). The reads and `readseq` are P,
   as stage information. This generalises the fact into data, which a reader
   could call R. The hidden variants decide whether it matters.
7. **The `b = s ++ c` evaluator in P08a.** Here conc's splitting direction is
   computed by a separate loop, not by conc. I classed it P under rules 15
   and 19: these are operations of the ++ encoding, and rule 19 says
   computing any place is P in every direction. Rule 14 (a separate
   direction function is R) would apply if this were read as a use of
   conc. The problem writes the stage with ++, so I did not read it that way.
8. **`same` and `sameel`** (the equality of the encoding) are P by rule 15.
   `sameel` treats two different unknown elements as unequal. No stage
   reaches that case.
9. **P07g's integer square root.** `entier(sqrt(c1) + 0.5)` is P, as a
   computation of the place x from c (rule 19). The built-ins sqrt and
   entier are core (3.2.4–5) and are listed under rule 9. `if nx > 0 then`
   is R, and `nx := 0` at the start is R ("x has no value").
10. **The program's outermost `begin … end`** is P, as the frame of the
    transcription (rule 1). The rules say nothing on it; H would also be
    defensible. It is 2 tokens per text.
11. **Rule 20 (separators).** A `;` goes to the construct after it. An `end`
    followed by its end-comment identifier (`end examine1`) is tokenised,
    and both tokens take the class of the compound's `begin`. A `begin` or
    `end` takes the class of the header that introduces it (rule 10).

## Outcomes

- All 45 behaviour records (3 configurations × 15 instances) are valid.
  None is `.INVALID`, none has a harness fault, a manual action or a safety
  stop, and there are no `raw-rerun-m2/` reruns. `rerun-m2-log.tsv` does not
  exist.
- x1 and x1sim agree with report on every stage, apart from the padding in
  integer printing.
- In report and x1, P08 is posed incrementally into a computation re-created
  for its budget. x1sim keeps one live process.
- **Cost and storage.** All 60 cost and storage runs agree with their
  behaviour runs in answers, states, observe text, suspended items and
  operation counts. So `mode_differences` is empty. The storage records'
  null peaks follow the harness's attribution rule (README 3.4): a peak is
  credited to a stage only where it exceeds the earlier one. They are not
  missing measurements.
- **Single-stage residuals (P07b, c, f).** Spec, Outcomes 2, counts a
  residual only if the program "holds and acts on [it] at a later stage",
  and a one-stage problem has no later stage. I counted them as reported:
  they are the program's holding structure, read by observe, which the
  mechanism would act on, and the problem file gives exactly these cases
  as *residual*. I also set **identical to the posed information** true.
  The rule is unclear for one-stage problems.
- **P07e** reports none: "no solution" in observe and no answer. I classed it
  *complete* / *explicit*, with simplification null. The table has no
  representation for an empty set reported as empty.
- **P08 readings.** In each P08 entry, `semantic` gives the open reading and
  `semantic_by_reading` gives both. At P08a/b stages 2–3 and P08c stages 2–3
  the result is *unsound* under the closed reading, because the program
  reports held solutions where that reading has none. The program never
  reports "none", so no conclusion is withdrawn at the stage where the
  definition arrives.
- **P08a stages 3–5** are *reducible*. x = y and y = z are held as
  relations to decide, not as identifications, and the solved form has
  none. equiv.py checks their equivalence by union-find.

## Files read outside the list

- None of the forbidden files was opened. I listed some directory names
  (the repository root, `programs/algol-60/`, `results/algol-60/` and its
  `report`/`x1`/`x1sim` folders). The listings showed that
  `results/algol-60/classes/`, `results/*/P0x.md` and
  `programs/algol-60/README.md` exist, but I read none of them.
- The session start showed the user's auto-memory index
  (`~/.claude/.../memory/MEMORY.md`, two lines about other matters). I did
  not open it, it bears on nothing here, and I note it only because the
  brief lists `~/.claude`.
- The brief's first paragraph says "batch 1A", but its title and paths say
  1B. I took it to be 1B.

## Summary

**Tokens** (16 texts, 17,531 tokens): P 3,409, R 3,160, H 10,962, C 0, S 0.

|---|---|---|---|
| report/P07a | 101 | 292 | 821 |

| report/P07c | 37 | 108 | 495 |

| report/P07f | 66 | 172 | 598 |

| report/P08a (and P08b) | 713 | 370 | 1502 |
| report/P08c | 455 | 209 | 784 |
| x1/P07a (and x1sim) | 92 | 292 | 741 |
| x1/P07b | 60 | 172 | 536 |
| x1/P07c | 34 | 108 | 443 |
| x1/P07d (and P07e, x1sim) | 131 | 212 | 664 |
| x1/P07f | 60 | 172 | 536 |

| x1/P08a (and P08b, x1sim) | 707 | 370 | 1372 |
| x1/P08c | 443 | 209 | 706 |

**Outcomes** (75 stage entries over 45 behaviour records): every stage is
reached and *complete* under the open reading.

| result | entries | which stages |

| explicit, finished | 33 | P07a in all six orders, P07d, P07e (none reported), P07g (both roots), P08a stage 6, P08c stage 4 |
| solved form, finished | 9 | P08a/b stage 1, P08c stage 1 |
| residual, reduced, suspended | 15 | P07c, P08a/b stage 2, P08c stages 2–3 |
| residual, reducible, suspended | 15 | P07b, P08a/b stage 3, P08a stages 4–5 |
| residual, inconsistency undetected, suspended | 3 | P07f |

- Under the closed reading, 18 P08 entries are *unsound*.
- No mode differences, harness faults, interventions or withdrawn conclusions.
- **Expressibility:** every P07 and P08 sub-problem is *expressible with
  reformulation* in all three configurations. The reformulation is the
  problem-specific holding code, R by rule 19. Only conc's forward
  direction in P08a/b is *expressible*.
- **Late definition:** all nine P08 programs take *permission awaited*:
  definition flags guard code that is already in the program.
- **S mechanisms:** none, in any program.
